---
title: "Speed and Scaling"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

Most of EDI's (Experimental Design and Inference) model fits run in compiled C++
and take well under a millisecond. Most of the waiting in a real analysis comes
from procedures that refit the model many times: randomization tests, bootstraps,
test-inversion confidence intervals, and simulation studies. This article covers
the settings that control that cost: parallel workers, a per-machine tuning
step, how the package was compiled, and the choice of procedure and replicate
count. It also summarizes how EDI's timings compare with other R packages,
including the cases where EDI is slower.

It assumes you know the four steps of an EDI analysis (design, assign, record
responses, infer) from [Get started](EDI.html).

## Parallelism

### `set_num_cores()` and per-object `num_cores`

EDI runs serially by default. `set_num_cores(k)` sets a package-wide budget of
`k` workers and starts a persistent worker pool: a fork cluster on Unix-alikes
(Linux, macOS), or `mirai` daemons on Windows or when you pass
`force_mirai = TRUE`. `unset_num_cores()` stops the pool and returns to serial
execution.

```{r cores-api, eval = FALSE}
set_num_cores(4)     # package-wide budget: 4 workers
# ... analyses ...
unset_num_cores()    # back to serial
```

Every inference object has a `num_cores` field. It reads the package-wide budget
unless you set it on that object, which overrides the budget for that object only:

```{r cores-field, eval = FALSE}
inf = InferenceContinOLS$new(des)
inf$num_cores          # the package-wide budget
inf$num_cores = 1L     # this object runs serially
```

Designs do not have their own setting; they use the package-wide budget.

### What runs in parallel

- **Randomization tests and intervals** (`compute_rand_two_sided_pval()`,
  `compute_rand_confidence_interval()`): the `r` redraws of the statistic are
  split across workers.
- **Bootstraps** (`compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval()`,
  `compute_bootstrap_two_sided_pval()` and the other resampling families): the
  `B` resamples are split across workers.
- **Design draws in native code.** `DesignFixedGreedy`,
  `DesignFixedMatchingGreedyPairSwitching`, `DesignFixedBinaryMatch`,
  `DesignFixedRerandomization`, `DesignFixedGreedyDOptimal` and
  `DesignFixedOptimal` run their searches in OpenMP threads, so both the
  allocation and the redraws a randomization test needs use the cores.
  `DesignFixedBlocking`, `DesignFixedOptimalBlocks`, `DesignFixedCluster` and
  `DesignFixedBlockedCluster` draw all `r` assignments in one vectorized pass in
  the main R process; extra cores do not change their speed or their draws.
- **`InferenceSuite$run_all_inference(num_cores = k)`** fits the applicable
  inference classes in parallel across `k` forked workers (Unix-alikes only; on
  other platforms it falls back to sequential with a warning).
- **`SimulationFramework$new(num_cores = k)`** runs Monte Carlo replications in
  parallel. While it does, parallelism inside each inference call is turned
  off so the machine is not oversubscribed.

More cores do not always help. Two rules keep EDI from using workers where
they are known to lose time:

- **A serial blocklist.** Workloads that were consistently slower with multiple
  workers in the package benchmarks always run serially: incidence
  randomization confidence intervals, bootstraps for incidence procedures,
  bootstraps for non-KK survival procedures, and bootstraps for one KK
  Wilcoxon class. `get_parallel_dispatch_policy()` shows the current list
  and `set_parallel_dispatch_policy()` changes it.
- **A warm-up check.** Before a parallel randomization run, EDI times one
  iteration. If `r` iterations would finish faster than the cost of sending
  them to the workers, it runs serially.

```{r dispatch-policy}
str(get_parallel_dispatch_policy())
```

### Reproducibility across core counts

Each parallel stream in EDI is seeded from the logical index of the draw or the
chunk, not from the worker that happens to compute it. With a seed set, a
randomization p-value or bootstrap interval is the same at 1, 2 or 8 cores. The
timing demo [below](#a-timing-demo) checks this with `identical()`.
`SimulationFramework` gives each replication its own seed (`seed + i`), so its
results do not depend on `num_cores` or on the fork or `mirai` backend.

Before version 1.0.4, seeded draws from the greedy, D-optimal, pair-switching
and rerandomization designs changed with the thread count. Version 1.0.4 fixed
this; those designs' seeded allocations changed once as a result (see `NEWS`).
A package-wide guarantee, with invariance tests across every class at
1, 2 and 4 cores on both backends and a reproducibility record attached to each
result, is planned under v1.1.0-TODO-48 and is not yet in place. If an exact
match across core counts matters for your analysis, check it with `identical()`
on your own design and procedure. `vignette("reproducibility")` explains the
seeding rules in full.

## Machine tuning

Several of EDI's performance defaults were chosen by timing them on the
maintainer's machine. These are speed choices only, never statistical ones:
whether a model fit starts from a quick OLS warm-up or from zero, whether
resampling reuses the previous replicate's solution as a starting point (and
up to what sample size), which optimizer a family uses, and at what sample
size parallel resampling starts to beat serial. The best choice depends on the
core count, caches, BLAS library and compiler flags, so it can differ on your
machine.

`tune_EDI_for_this_machine()` repeats those timings on your hardware.

```{r tune, eval = FALSE}
tune_EDI_for_this_machine()                    # "standard": about 3-4 hours
tune_EDI_for_this_machine(effort = "quick")    # about 1 hour
tune_EDI_for_this_machine(dry_run = TRUE)      # benchmark, but save and apply nothing
```

The duration estimates are the ones the function prints; they were measured on
a 6-core laptop. `effort = "thorough"` has not been timed; plan on running it
overnight.

**What is measured.** Four axes: the cold-start setting, the warm-start setting
for each resampling operation, the optimizer algorithm (only when you supply a
`converged_fn` that reports whether a fit converged), and the parallel-versus-serial
crossover sample size (Unix-alikes with at least 2 cores). For each inference
family and sample size, both settings are timed on the same synthetic data. A
setting replaces the shipped default only if its median time is at least 5%
better and the improvement exceeds twice its own interquartile range. Each
accepted change is then refit once under both settings, and it is discarded if
the results disagree. The bootstrap interval type and the serial blocklist
above are never tuned.

**Run it on an idle machine.** A tuning run on a busy machine measures the
contention, not the hardware. The function checks the load average and the
noise in a short calibration timing first, and refuses to run if the machine
looks busy (in an interactive session it asks first), unless you pass
`force = TRUE`.

**Where it is stored.** The result is written to `machine_policies.rds` in
`tools::R_user_dir("EDI", which = "config")`, a per-user directory, and applied
immediately. Every later `library(EDI)` applies it again.

```{r tune-manage, eval = FALSE}
get_local_EDI_optimization()     # print what is saved; changes nothing
clear_local_EDI_optimization()   # delete the saved file and restore the shipped defaults
```

To ignore a saved tuning for one session without deleting it, set the
environment variable `EDI_SKIP_LOCAL_TUNING=1` before `library(EDI)`. This is
useful for checking whether the tuning is behind a timing difference you see.

**The core count is never applied for you.** The parallel axis records the
core count that was fastest, but EDI never changes the core count at load time.
If a saved tuning includes one, `library(EDI)` prints a startup message:

```
EDI: this machine's saved tuning found parallel execution fastest at 2 cores.
This is not applied automatically -- call set_num_cores(2) to opt in.
```

Call `set_num_cores()` with that number if you want it.

**The fingerprint and when to re-tune.** The saved file records the machine it
was measured on: logical and physical core counts, CPU model, vendor and
architecture, RAM, BLAS and LAPACK libraries, R version and platform,
operating system, and the build of EDI itself (portable or native, link-time
optimization, compiler and compiler flags; see [Builds](#builds)). At load, EDI
compares only the logical core count and the CPU model. If either differs, it
still applies the saved settings but prints a message suggesting a re-run.
EDI does not detect the other changes, so re-run `tune_EDI_for_this_machine()`
yourself (it overwrites the old file) after:

- moving to different hardware,
- reinstalling EDI with different build flags (for example, switching to or
  from the native build),
- changing your BLAS library, or
- upgrading EDI, since the shipped defaults themselves may have changed.

## Builds

EDI's C++ code can be compiled in two ways.

- **Portable** (`EDI_PORTABLE=1`, the default). This is the build CRAN and
  R-universe ship, and also what you get from a source install such as
  `remotes::install_github()` or `install.packages(type = "source")`. It uses
  only R's standard compiler flags, so it runs on any CPU of the target
  architecture, and the same seed gives the same results on Linux, macOS and
  Windows.
- **Native** (`EDI_PORTABLE=0`, opt-in, source installs only). The `configure`
  script adds `-march=native -mtune=native` (every vector instruction set the
  build machine supports) and forces `-O3`. Link-time optimization stays off
  unless you also set `EDI_NATIVE_LTO=1`, because LTO builds have slowed some of
  the small model-fit kernels considerably.

```{r native-build, eval = FALSE}
# Not run: a native build compiles the whole package and takes several minutes.
Sys.setenv(EDI_PORTABLE = "0")
remotes::install_github("kapelner/EDI", subdir = "R/EDI")
```

The tradeoff: the native build can be faster, but the binary runs only on
CPUs like the one it was compiled on, and floating-point results can differ in
the last bits from the portable build. Seeded results from a native build may
therefore not match a colleague's CRAN install exactly. If you change build,
re-run the machine tuning.

`edi_build_info_cpp()` reports how the loaded copy of EDI was compiled. The
values are fixed when the shared library is built. The fields below are the
ones that matter for speed (the full list also includes the build machine's
host name and R installation path):

```{r build-info}
info = edi_build_info_cpp()
str(info[c("env_edi_portable", "env_edi_native_lto", "pkg_cxxflags",
           "compiler", "compiler_optimize_macro", "compiler_fast_math_macro",
           "eigen_dont_vectorize_macro")])
```

`env_edi_portable` is `"1"` for the portable build and `"0"` for the native one.

## How EDI compares

EDI's benchmark suite runs nightly on a GitHub-hosted Linux runner. The
numbers below come from the report published on
[the benchmarks page](https://kapelner.github.io/EDI/benchmarks/) on
2026-11-17 (timed 2026-11-16 and 2026-11-17 UTC at EDI commit `7d906456f26f`;
report commit `1d407fae` on the `benchmark-results` branch). That run used the
portable build (`EDI_PORTABLE=1`), R 4.6.2 and g++ 15.2.0. The numbers will
change as the code changes; the page has the current run and full tables.
"Speedup" is the other package's time divided by EDI's time, so values below 1
mean EDI was slower.

### Model fits and Wald inference

These tables time EDI's compiled kernels against the lowest-level function each
comparison package exposes (`lm.fit`, `glm.fit`, `coxph.fit`, `MASS::glm.nb`,
`MASS::rlm`, `betareg`, `pscl`, `ordinal::clm`, `VGAM::vglm`, `lme4`,
`glmmTMB` and others), with design matrices built outside the timed region on
both sides. They time the numerical work only. They do **not** include
constructing an EDI inference object, which took about 0.7 to 1.8 ms in the
procedure benchmarks below. For a single fit, that construction cost can be
larger than the fit itself; the [timing demo](#a-timing-demo) shows this for
OLS.

The full-inference table (fit, standard error and Wald p-value, $n = 200$)
summarized by response type:

```{r bench-wald, echo = FALSE}
wald = data.frame(
  `Response type`    = c("continuous", "incidence", "count", "proportion", "survival", "ordinal"),
  `Comparisons`      = c(12, 11, 11, 3, 9, 8),
  `Median speedup`   = c("19x", "11x", "29x", "50x", "21x", "14x"),
  `Smallest speedup` = c("1.0x (quantreg `rq`)", "1.2x (`fisher.test`)", "8.1x (glmmTMB Poisson GLMM)",
                         "26x (`glm` quasi + g-computation)", "1.05x (`survfit` median)",
                         "3.3x (clinfun `jonckheere`)"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(wald)
```

EDI's kernel was faster in all 54 comparisons, by a median of 21x. In 52 of
them the difference was significant at the 5% level. The two that were not are
quantile regression against `quantreg` (1.0x: EDI uses the same algorithm) and
the Kaplan-Meier median difference against `survival::survfit` (1.05x). The
point-estimate-only table ($n = 1{,}000$; 500 for survival) is similar: EDI was
faster in all 50 comparisons, by a median of 14x, with quantile regression
again the only non-significant one. The largest ratios come from comparisons
against general-purpose fitters, such as a Weibull frailty model against
`parfm` and Gaussian mixed models against `glmmTMB`.

### Resampling procedures

The procedure table times complete calls ($n = 1{,}000$; 500 for Cox), with
$r = 1{,}000$ randomizations or $B = 1{,}000$ (OLS) or $500$ (logistic, Cox)
bootstrap draws on both sides, and percentile bootstrap intervals on both sides.
"R6" rows go through the public inference classes, the way you would call
them. "Kernel" rows call EDI's C++ kernel directly.

```{r bench-procedures, echo = FALSE}
proc = data.frame(
  Procedure = c(
    "Randomization p-value, mean difference",
    "Randomization p-value, mean difference",
    "Randomization p-value, mean difference",
    "Randomization p-value, mean difference",
    "Randomization p-value, OLS with covariates",
    "Bootstrap CI, OLS",
    "Bootstrap CI, OLS",
    "Bootstrap CI, logistic regression",
    "Bootstrap CI, Cox model",
    "Exact Fisher 2x2 p-value",
    "Exact CI for the log odds ratio"),
  `EDI path` = c("R6 `InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff`", "R6 `InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff`",
                 "kernel", "kernel",
                 "R6 `InferenceContinOLS`",
                 "R6 `InferenceContinOLS`", "kernel (not used by any class yet)",
                 "R6 `InferenceIncidLogRegr`", "R6 `InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr`",
                 "kernel", "R6 `InferenceIncidExactZhang`"),
  `EDI (ms)` = c(43.5, 41.7, 3.65, 3.42, 39.8, 1616, 13.9, 550.5, 353, 0.03, 1.74),
  Comparison = c("coin `oneway_test`", "ri2 `conduct_ri`", "coin `oneway_test`", "ri2 `conduct_ri`",
                 "ri2 `conduct_ri`", "boot + `boot.ci`", "boot + `boot.ci`", "boot + `boot.ci`",
                 "boot + `boot.ci`", "`fisher.test`", "`fisher.test(conf.int = TRUE)`"),
  `Comparison (ms)` = c(8.84, 932, 8.31, 946.5, 971.5, 105, 105, 516.5, 148, 0.70, 0.56),
  Speedup = c("0.20x", "22x", "2.3x", "277x", "24x", "0.065x", "7.5x", "0.94x (not significant)",
              "0.42x", "22x", "0.32x"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(proc)
```

The R6 resampling paths carry a lot of overhead. EDI's mean-difference kernel
is about 2.3 times faster than `coin`, but the same test called through
`InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff` is about 5 times slower than `coin`. The OLS
bootstrap through `InferenceContinOLS` took about 15 times as long as `boot`.
EDI has a compiled OLS bootstrap kernel that beats `boot` by 7.5x, but no
inference class calls it yet. The Cox bootstrap was about 2.4 times slower than
`boot`, the logistic bootstrap was about even, and the exact interval from
`InferenceIncidExactZhang` took about 3 times as long as `fisher.test()`. EDI's
randomization tests are 22 to 24 times faster than `ri2`, and the randomization
confidence intervals (about 0.1 s for test inversion at $r = 1{,}000$) have no
counterpart in `ri2`, `coin` or `perm` to compare against.

### Designs

Producing one allocation of $n = 1{,}000$ subjects. "Total" includes
constructing the design and adding the covariates; the reported speedup uses
the assignment step only.

```{r bench-designs, echo = FALSE}
des_tab = data.frame(
  Design = c("`DesignFixediBCRD` (complete randomization)",
             "`DesignFixedBlocking` (6 blocks)",
             "`DesignFixedBinaryMatch` (optimal pairs, 4 covariates)",
             "`DesignFixedBinaryMatch` (optimal pairs, 4 covariates)",
             "`DesignSeqOneByOnePocockSimon` (1,000 arrivals)",
             "`DesignSeqOneByOnePocockSimon` (1,000 arrivals)"),
  `EDI total (ms)` = c(0.61, 1.12, 208.5, 203.8, 168.5, 167.5),
  `EDI assignment (ms)` = c(0.04, 0.50, 205.5, 201.0, 166.5, 166.0),
  Comparison = c("randomizr `complete_ra`", "randomizr `block_ra`",
                 "nbpMatching (optimal)", "blockTools (greedy)",
                 "carat `PocSimMIN`", "Minirand (R loop)"),
  `Comparison (ms)` = c(0.11, 0.34, 277, 240, 3.21, 795.5),
  Speedup = c("2.7x", "0.68x", "1.35x (not significant)", "1.19x (not significant)", "0.019x", "4.8x"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(des_tab)
```

`randomizr` is faster end to end for simple designs. EDI's assignment step for
complete randomization is quicker, but constructing the design object brings
EDI's total to about 5 times `randomizr`'s, and blocking is slower even in the
assignment step. Optimal matching is about even with `nbpMatching`, which EDI
calls for the matching itself. Pocock-Simon minimization is about 50 times
slower than `carat`, which runs the whole arrival sequence in one C++ call;
EDI processes each arrival through a separate method call, the way a
sequential trial enrolls subjects. It is still about 5 times faster than
`Minirand`.

In short, EDI's model fitting is fast, but each R6 inference object carries a
fixed cost on the order of a millisecond or more (the [timing demo](#a-timing-demo) measures
it on the machine that built this page), and several resampling and design
paths are slower than the dedicated packages. If raw speed for one of those
procedures is the main concern, the packages above are good choices.

## Practical tips

### Cheap and expensive procedures

Costs for one inference object, from cheapest to most expensive:

1. **Asymptotic procedures** (`compute_asymp_confidence_interval()`,
   `compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()`, and the score, likelihood-ratio and
   gradient versions): one fit, or a few for the score and likelihood-ratio
   intervals, which invert a test. Milliseconds. Use these for screening many
   models or settings.
2. **Exact procedures** (for example `InferenceIncidExactFisher`): fast for 2x2
   tables.
3. **Randomization p-values**: `r` redraws from the design plus `r` refits.
   Redraws are cheap for most designs and expensive for search-based designs
   such as `DesignFixedGreedy`, `DesignFixedRerandomization` and
   `DesignFixedOptimal`.
4. **Randomization confidence intervals**: invert the test, so they evaluate
   the p-value at several effect sizes. In the benchmarks above, the interval
   took about 3 times as long as one p-value at the same `r`.
5. **Bootstrap intervals**: `B` refits. The default interval type for most
   classes is BCa (`get_bootstrap_dispatch_policy()$default_type`), which also
   runs a leave-one-out jackknife ($n$ more refits). `type = "percentile"`
   skips the jackknife. Double and calibrated bootstraps nest a second level of
   resampling and cost far more.

### Choosing `r` and `B`

The defaults are $r = 501$ and $B = 501$. A resampling p-value is a Monte Carlo
estimate. Its standard error is about $\sqrt{p(1-p)/r}$, where $p$ is the
p-value you would get with unlimited draws:

```{r mc-error}
mc_se = function(p, r) sqrt(p * (1 - p) / r)
r_grid = c(101, 501, 1999, 9999)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  r = r_grid,
  `MC SE at p = 0.05` = round(mc_se(0.05, r_grid), 4),
  `MC SE at p = 0.5`  = round(mc_se(0.5, r_grid), 4),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

Near $p = 0.05$, the default $r = 501$ gives a standard error of about
`r round(mc_se(0.05, 501), 3)`, so a reported p-value of 0.04 or 0.06 cannot be
reliably placed on either side of 0.05. For a final result near your
threshold, use `r` in the thousands. Halving the standard error takes four
times as many draws, and four times the run time. Bootstrap interval
endpoints are noisy quantile estimates with no comparably simple formula;
re-run with a different seed and check that the interval does not move by an
amount you care about. Use small `r` and `B` while you develop code, and large
ones for the reported analysis.

### `InferenceSuite`: limit methods and time

`InferenceSuite$run_all_inference()` runs every applicable class and method by
default, including the resampling methods at full replicate counts, which can
take minutes. (Paths known to be very slow, listed in
`EDI_COMPREHENSIVE_SLOW_PATHS`, are left out unless you request them.) Three
arguments keep it manageable:

- `methods = c("wald", "score", "lik_ratio")` runs only asymptotic methods, a
  quick first pass.
- `max_secs_per_class = 30` stops any class that runs longer than 30 seconds
  and marks its row `"timeout"`. R checks the limit only between R-level
  operations, so one long call into compiled code can overrun it.
- `classes =` and `exclude_classes =` choose which classes to fit.

```{r suite, eval = FALSE}
suite = InferenceSuite$new(des)
res = suite$run_all_inference(methods = c("wald", "score", "lik_ratio"),
                              max_secs_per_class = 30)
```

### `show_progress`

The resampling methods print a progress bar by default
(`show_progress = TRUE`). It does not affect the result. Set
`show_progress = FALSE` in scripts, R Markdown documents and simulation loops.

### A timing demo

A small count-response trial: 300 subjects, three covariates, complete
randomization, and a negative binomial model. We time one OLS model fit, then a
randomization p-value ($r = 500$) and a percentile bootstrap interval
($B = 500$) at 1 core and at 2 cores, with the same seed both times. Your
timings will differ: they depend on the machine, its load, and the build.

```{r demo-data}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 300
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n))
des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "count", verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des$get_w()
des$add_all_subject_responses(rnbinom(n, size = 2, mu = exp(1 + 0.3 * w + 0.5 * X$x1)))
```

First, the fixed cost of a single fit through an inference object. We fit OLS
on a continuous response with the same covariates, through `InferenceContinOLS`
and through a bare `lm.fit()` on a prebuilt matrix:

```{r demo-fit}
des_ols = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", verbose = FALSE)
des_ols$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_ols$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
y_ols = 1 + 0.3 * des_ols$get_w() + X$x1 + rnorm(n)
des_ols$add_all_subject_responses(y_ols)
Xmat = cbind(1, w = des_ols$get_w(), as.matrix(X))

InferenceContinOLS$new(des_ols, verbose = FALSE)$compute_estimate()   # warm-up, not timed
t_edi = system.time(for (i in 1:20) {
  InferenceContinOLS$new(des_ols, verbose = FALSE)$compute_estimate()
})[["elapsed"]] / 20
t_lmfit = system.time(for (i in 1:200) lm.fit(Xmat, y_ols))[["elapsed"]] / 200
round(1000 * c(InferenceContinOLS = t_edi, lm.fit = t_lmfit), 3)   # milliseconds per fit
```

Constructing the object and fitting took `r round(1000 * t_edi, 1)` ms, against
`r round(1000 * t_lmfit, 2)` ms for `lm.fit()`. The object's fixed cost
(checking the design, building the model matrix, setting up caches) is
negligible for one analysis, but it adds up when you construct thousands of
objects in a loop.

Now the resampling procedures at 1 and 2 cores. `clear_randomization_cache()`
makes sure each run draws its own permutations rather than reusing the cached
ones.

```{r demo-cores}
run_resampling = function(k) {
  inf = InferenceCountNegBin$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
  inf$num_cores = k
  inf$set_seed(1)
  inf$clear_randomization_cache()
  t_rand = system.time(
    p <- inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
  )[["elapsed"]]
  t_boot = system.time(
    ci <- inf$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(B = 500, type = "percentile",
                                                    show_progress = FALSE)
  )[["elapsed"]]
  list(time = c(rand_pval = t_rand, bootstrap_ci = t_boot), p = p, ci = ci)
}

invisible(run_resampling(1L))   # warm-up, not timed: first calls pay one-time costs
one = run_resampling(1L)
set_num_cores(2)
two = run_resampling(2L)
unset_num_cores()

rbind(`1 core` = one$time, `2 cores` = two$time)   # seconds
c(rand_pval_identical = identical(one$p, two$p),
  bootstrap_ci_identical = identical(one$ci, two$ci))
```

The randomization p-value is `r one$p` and the bootstrap interval is
(`r round(one$ci[1], 3)`, `r round(one$ci[2], 3)`)
`r if (identical(one$p, two$p) && identical(one$ci, two$ci)) "at both core counts" else "at 1 core; the 2-core run differed (see the check above)"`.
On the machine that built this page, the 2-core run took
`r round(100 * two$time[["rand_pval"]] / one$time[["rand_pval"]])`% of the 1-core
time for the randomization test and
`r round(100 * two$time[["bootstrap_ci"]] / one$time[["bootstrap_ci"]])`% for the
bootstrap. A second core can at best about halve the time, and starting and
feeding the workers takes a share of a run this small. Parallelism pays off when each refit is expensive, when `r` or `B` is in
the thousands, or for a simulation study run through `SimulationFramework`.
Time your own workload at the core counts you are considering, or let
`tune_EDI_for_this_machine()` measure the crossover for you.
